idiom_name: AtLeastOnceDelivery with deliver/confirmDelivery over a PersistentActor journal
implementation_notes: Scala's actor stack absorbs the pattern: mixing AtLeastOnceDelivery into a PersistentActor (or extending AbstractPersistentActorWithAtLeastOnceDelivery) makes the journal the durable store, deliver(destination)(id => message) the store-and-forward step, and confirmDelivery(deliveryId) - sent by the destination as a reply - the acknowledgement that stops re-sending. Unconfirmed deliveries are retried after a configurable interval and warnAfterNumberOfUnconfirmedAttempts flags the ones that never confirm, so the replay logic is the framework's rather than yours. The destination must be idempotent (at-least-once is explicit in the name); choose the Kafka variant instead when the store should be a shared broker log rather than the actor's journal.
pitfalls: The destination must reply with the deliveryId and the sender must translate that reply into confirmDelivery; otherwise every message is re-sent forever.
Delivery tracking is actor state: unconfirmed messages accumulate (bounded only by max-unconfirmed-messages), so a dead destination must be alerted on, not just retried.
At-least-once means the receiver sees duplicates after every crash-restart window; idempotence in the destination is mandatory.
The typed EventSourcedBehavior API has no equivalent of AtLeastOnceDelivery - a typed service needs the retry/outbox or the classic actor API, and mixing them is a design decision, not a drop-in.

variants.name: Kafka transactional producer from Scala
variants.implementation_notes: Scala backends use the JVM Kafka client directly: enable.idempotence=true for retry-safe writes plus a transaction so the produced records and the consumed offsets commit together (sendOffsetsToTransaction), which is the acknowledgement protocol for consume-transform-produce. The broker log is the store and the transaction is what the Pekko variant achieves with a journal plus explicit confirmations; choose Kafka when the data must be visible to other services on a shared topic. The blocking KafkaProducer belongs behind a dedicated dispatcher or an Akka Streams/Pekko Streams producer stage.
pitfalls: KafkaProducer blocks and is not stream-aware: calling it on the actor/stream dispatcher stalls the whole system - isolate it.
A transaction left open (no commit or abort on an exception path) blocks the transactional id until transaction.timeout.ms.
Consumers must use isolation.level=read_committed, otherwise records from aborted transactions are delivered - Scala clients default to read_uncommitted.
One transactional id must map to exactly one live producer instance; a rolling restart without fencing can let two instances write.
